newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan begins U.N. reform with staff, budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Annan begins U.N. reform with staff, budget cuts.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, with an eye on the U.S. Congress, announced staff and budget cuts on Monday as the first step in his programme to reform and restructure the United Nations.

Annan, in a statement to be followed by a news conference, revealed his so-called "track one" initiatives that could be enacted immediately. They are to be followed up by another, fuller report in July.
"I am convinced that through these reforms we can do even more good, even more efficiently in this era of challenge and expectation," he said.
-- A reduction of 1,000 staff posts for the secretariat or core U.N. staff, which has about 9,000 employees based primarily in New York, Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi.
-- Budget cuts of $123 million for 1998-1999. The 1997 current budget is about $1.3 billion annually, about the same amount as the U.S. debt to the world body for dues and peacekeeping.
-- Consolidating three departments dealing with economic and social issues.
-- Streamlining technical support and reducing documents by 25 percent in 1998.
Annan said 38 percent of the organisation's resources were devoted to administration. He said he was committed to reducing this by a third.
But he also made clear that some of the money saved would be channelled into resources for economic and social programmes in the developing world, rather than just reduce members' dues.

The secretary-general took office on Jan. 1 after the United States last year vetoed his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, for allegedly not doing enough for reform. The conservative U.S. Congress has vowed not to pay the $1 billion Washington owes the world body until it was satisfied with Annan's reform programme.

U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson was quick to compliment Annan: "This plan shows that the secretary-general has answered the call for leadership on reform and is prepared to exercise the powers of his office in an affirmative and appropriate manner," he said.
Richardson, however, said he recognised that many of the "broader, structural and organisational reforms" must be negotiated with other U.N. members.

Annan limited his initial proposals to the secretariat, which he controls. Another estimated 40,000 people are employed by a network of specialised U.N. agencies, which have their own boards and fund-raising procedures. He expects to make proposals on their activities in June.
But many have doubts the right-wing U.S. Congress will approve the funds to save the world body from bankruptcy.

Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, head of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, is expected to insist on drastic cost-cutting of at least a fourth of the staff, conditions which have angered other U.N. members, particularly the 15-nation European Community that pays most of the U.N. bills.
